What changes: You are building the platform, not testing it. Four weeks of aerobic volume, ski technique and strength accumulation. Nothing here should feel maximal.
One priority: Benchmark carefully in Week 1, since every number you record now is what the following eleven weeks are measured against.
If you miss a session: Drop it and move on. Nothing in this phase is irreplaceable, and doubling up usually costs more than the missed session was worth. If two are missed in a week, repeating the week is the better option.
Looking ahead: Week 2 adds roughly ten per cent across the board. Same shape, more of it.

What changes: Volume climbs again. The ski work stays continuous rather than intervalled - you are learning to move efficiently before you learn to move fast.
One priority: Ski stroke rate. Hold 34-42 and drive from the hip. If your arms burn before your trunk does, you are pulling with your arms.
If you miss a session: Drop it and move on. Nothing in this phase is irreplaceable, and doubling up usually costs more than the missed session was worth. If two are missed in a week, repeating the week is the better option.
Looking ahead: Week 3 is the biggest week of the Base phase. Ski reaches twenty-five minutes continuous.

What changes: The biggest week of the phase. Strength volume peaks and ski time reaches twenty-five minutes continuous. Hold technique as fatigue arrives.
One priority: Technique under fatigue. The last five minutes of every ski and the last set of every lift are where the phase is won.
If you miss a session: Drop it and move on. Nothing in this phase is irreplaceable, and doubling up usually costs more than the missed session was worth. If two are missed in a week, repeating the week is the better option.
Looking ahead: Week 4 is a deload. Volume drops by about forty per cent and the shape of the week stays intact.

What changes: Deload. Volume drops by roughly forty per cent while the shape of the week stays intact. Resist the urge to fill the gap.
One priority: Do less. The reduced load is what makes the next phase productive.
If you miss a session: Drop it and move on. Nothing in this phase is irreplaceable, and doubling up usually costs more than the missed session was worth. If two are missed in a week, repeating the week is the better option.
Looking ahead: Week 5 opens the Development phase. Ski becomes intervals, running becomes threshold, and the repeat-triple protocol starts.

What changes: Base is finished. Three things change at once. Ski moves from steady state to threshold intervals. Running moves to 3 km-specific intensity. Strength moves to heavy low-rep work and the repeat-triple protocol starts.
One priority: Wednesday's deadlift gap. Record both triples. Shrinking the difference between them is worth more score than adding weight to the first.
If you miss a session: Tuesday and Saturday are the ones to protect, since ski work and the run-to-ski transition have no direct substitute. The rest can be dropped without much cost.

What changes: Load climbs on all three fronts. The repeat-triple gap should already be shrinking. If it is widening, you are opening too heavy.
One priority: Ski interval consistency. The drop from the first interval to the last matters more than how fast the first one was.
If you miss a session: Tuesday and Saturday are the ones to protect, since ski work and the run-to-ski transition have no direct substitute. The rest can be dropped without much cost.

What changes: Peak week of the phase, and the first full rehearsal of the Endurance Zone on Saturday. Treat that session as data collection, not a workout.
One priority: Saturday's rehearsal. Run the buy-in at the pace you intend to race and record every 500 m ski split.

What changes: Deload before the specific phase. Intensity stays, volume halves. You are clearing fatigue to arrive sharp, not losing fitness.
One priority: Arrive at Week 9 recovered, since the Specific phase depends on it.
If you miss a session: Tuesday and Saturday are the ones to protect, since ski work and the run-to-ski transition have no direct substitute. The rest can be dropped without much cost.
Looking ahead: Week 9 opens the Specific phase. Everything now runs at competition pace, weight and timing.

What changes: Everything now happens at competition pace, weight and timing. Wednesday's lift becomes the full strength sequence against the clock. Saturday becomes a zone simulation.
One priority: Derive your entry pace. Compare this week's Endurance rehearsal against Week 7 and commit to the faster total.
If you miss a session: Saturday is the one to protect. The zone simulations produce the data you need to set your race strategy, so it is worth moving the rest of the week around them.

If you miss a session: Saturday is the one to protect. The zone simulations produce the data you need to set your race strategy, so it is worth moving the rest of the week around them.

What changes: Final build. One full competition simulation on Saturday, then the unload begins. After this week you do not add fitness, you only preserve it.

Looking ahead: Week 12 is the taper. Volume drops hard, intensity holds, and eccentric work stops.

What changes: Volume drops sharply while intensity holds. Heavy eccentric work stops seven days out, since it is the main cause of lingering soreness. Everything this week is intended to let the previous eleven weeks show.
One priority: Doing less than you feel like doing is the aim this week. The work is already done.
If you miss a session: Miss whatever you need to this week. Nothing here builds fitness, and arriving fresh matters more than arriving complete.
Looking ahead: Nothing. This is the week. Execute what you rehearsed and take no unnecessary risk in any zone.
